extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claims recite 'significantly more' than a judicial exception under the Alice/Mayo two-part test, including considerations for improvements to technology, particular machines, particular transformations, and whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to any other technology or technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements in technology beyond computer functionality may demonstrate patent eligibility. Claims directed to an improvement in a technological process (e.g., computer animation) are less likely to be directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basis: McRO held that claimed methods of automatic lip synchronization and facial expression animation using computer-implemented rules were patent eligible because they were directed to an improvement in computer animation rather than an abstract idea. To show that the involvement of a computer assists in improving the technology, the claims must recite the details regarding how a computer aids the method, the extent to which the computer aids the method, or the significance of a computer to the performance of the method. Merely adding generic computer components to perform the method is not sufficient. The claim must include more than mere instructions to perform the method on a generic component or machinery to qualify as an improvement to an existing technology. Examples the courts have indicated may be sufficient to show an improvement include: (i) a particular computerized method of operating a rubber molding press (Diamond v. Diehr), (ii) new telephone/server combinations (TLI Communications), (iii) advances in downloading for streaming (Affinity Labs v. DirecTV), (iv) improved methods of digital data compression (DDR Holdings), (v) methods for incorporating virus screening into the Internet (Symantec), (vi) components/methods that generate new data (Electric Power Group v. Alstom), (vii) particular configurations of inertial sensors (Thales Visionix), (viii) a specific, structured GUI that improves trader transaction accuracy (Trading Techs.), and (ix) improved biological preservation processes (Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect). Examples that may not be sufficient include commonplace business methods on a general purpose computer (Alice), use of well-known laboratory techniques to detect enzymes (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health), gathering/analyzing information using conventional techniques and displaying results (TLI Communications), delivering broadcast content to portable devices at a high level of generality (Affinity Labs), general methods of screening emails on a generic computer (Symantec), and selecting generic functions for hardware to perform (Affinity Labs). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for more on 'mere instructions to apply an exception.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Machine (machine-or-transformation test as a clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claim recites significantly more than a judicial exception, consider whether the judicial exception is applied with, or by use of, a particular machine. The machine-or-transformation (M-or-T) test is a useful clue and investigative tool but is not a stand-alone test for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General points: All claims must be evaluated using the Alice/Mayo two-part test. A claim that passes Alice/Mayo is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test; a claim that fails Alice/Mayo is ineligible even if it passes the M-or-T test. Examiners should consider other Step 2B factors (mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use/technological environment) when deciding whether a recited machine provides significantly more. Relevant factors when determining whether a recited machine or apparatus provides significantly more include: I. The particularity or generality of the elements of the machine or apparatus — whether the machine can be specifically identified (not any and all machines). Example: Mackay Radio (specific antenna details) and Eibel Process (Fourdrinier machine arranged in a particular way). Note that a general purpose computer applying a judicial exception using conventional computer functions does not qualify as a particular machine (Ultramercial v. Hulu). II. Whether the machine or apparatus implements the steps of the method — integral use of a machine to achieve performance may provide significantly more, whereas a machine that is merely an object on which the method operates generally does not (CyberSource v. Retail Decisions). If the machine only functions as an obvious mechanism to permit a solution to be achieved more quickly, it likely does not add significantly more (Versata v. SAP). III. Whether its involvement is extra-solution activity or a field-of-use — if the machine contributes only nominally or insignificantly (e.g., mere data-gathering or field-of-use limitations), it would not provide significantly more (Bilski; CyberSource). See MPEP §§ 2106.05(f), 2106.05(g), and 2106.05(h) for additional related considerations, and MPEP § 2106.03 for the definition of 'machine.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Transformation (machine-or-transformation test clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Another consideration for determining whether a claim recites significantly more is whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing. Transformation and reduction of an article to a different state or thing is a clue to patentability for process claims that do not include particular machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General points: The transformation of an article is an important clue but not a stand-alone test; evaluate claims under Alice/Mayo. An 'article' includes a physical object or substance and must be particular (specifically identifiable). 'Transformation' means the article has changed to a different state or thing — usually more than mere use or change in location; a new/different function or use can be evidence of transformation. Purely mental processes are not considered an eligible transformation; for data, mere manipulation of basic mathematical constructs (the paradigmatic 'abstract idea') is not a transformation. Example of transformation: Tilghman v. Proctor (transforming fatty bodies into fat acids and glycerine); Diamond v. Diehr (transforming raw, uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded products). Where a transformation is recited, consider these factors in the 'significantly more' analysis: 1. The particularity or generality of the transformation — more particular transformations likely provide significantly more. 2. The degree to which the recited article is particular — transformations applied to generically recited articles or 'any and all' articles likely do not provide significantly more. 3. The nature of the transformation in terms of the type/extent of change — transformations resulting in different function or use are more likely to provide significantly more than mere relocation. 4. The nature of the article transformed — physical/tangible object/substance transformations are more likely to provide significantly more than transformations of intangible concepts. 5. Whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or field-of-use — if the transformation contributes only nominally or insignificantly (e.g., a data-gathering step or field-of-use limitation), it will likely not provide significantly more (Mayo example). See MPEP §§ 2106.05(f), 2106.05(g), and 2106.05(h) for related considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether additional element(s) in a claim are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry. If the additional elements are merely well-understood, routine, conventional activities recited at a high level of generality, this consideration does not favor eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General guidance: If the additional element(s) are specific limitations that are unconventional or confine the claim to a particular useful application of the judicial exception, this favors eligibility (example: DDR Holdings — claims to generating a composite webpage that modified conventional hyperlink protocol). Conversely, if the additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities (example: Mayo — measuring metabolites using any known process), they do not amount to an inventive concept. Points for examiners when making this determination: I. An additional element known in the art can still be unconventional or non-routine — novelty/obviousness inquiries are distinct from eligibility. For example, Enfish claims were eligible because they recited non-conventional self-referential database features that improved technology even though some features were anticipated in prior art. II. A prior art search should not be necessary to resolve whether an additional element is well-understood, routine, conventional. Examiners should rely on what courts have recognized or what those in the art would recognize as widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant industry. An examiner should only conclude an element is well-understood/routine/conventional when they can readily conclude, based on their expertise in the art, that the element is widely prevalent or commonly used. If the element is not widely prevalent or is beyond elements recognized in the art or by courts as conventional, the element will in most cases favor eligibility. Note overlap with other Step 2B considerations (improvement, mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity) — evaluating those may assist in this determination.
